steps.say: Three developers work on one e-commerce app: login, shopping cart and payments.
Combined without checks, their changes can clash: incompatible code, missing dependencies, unexpected bugs.
Without automation, every update means installing, testing, building and deploying by hand: slow and error-prone.
CI/CD automates this. A pipeline connects every code change to validation, building and deployment.
Continuous Integration means merging changes into a shared repository often and validating every change automatically.
Every push or pull request starts the same automated steps.
Example: a React developer pushes a login update, and CI installs, tests and builds it.
term: CI: npm install · npm test · npm run build

steps.say: If a test fails, the developer gets feedback before the change is merged into main.
Continuous Delivery keeps every successfully tested change in a releasable state.
The production release can still wait for a manual approval.
Continuous Deployment skips the approval: changes that pass every required check go to production automatically.
A pipeline moves code from source to a running environment. It starts with source, build and test.
Code-quality checks and packaging into an artifact or container image follow.
Finally the application is deployed to a target environment and monitored for errors and performance.
Not every pipeline has exactly these stages: they depend on the technology stack and deployment needs.
A basic Node.js CI workflow runs three commands. First it installs the dependencies.
npm test runs the automated tests.
npm run build builds the application, if a build script is configured.
A deployment workflow can then publish the build to a hosting environment.
A green build alone does not mean production-ready: tests, security checks and runtime validation matter too.

wn.text: A green build is not enough

steps.say: Developers keep pushing changes. Someone must download, install, test and prepare each one, which is inefficient by hand.
Jenkins is an open-source automation server that runs builds, tests, code analysis, packaging and deployments.
A large plugin ecosystem connects Jenkins to Git, Docker, Kubernetes and SonarQube.
Jenkins uses a controller-agent architecture. The controller coordinates: web UI, scheduling, configuration.
Agents are the machines that do the actual build and test work the controller assigns.
A Docker image build is sent to the agent that has Docker installed.
Key terms: a job is a configured task, a build is one run, a plugin adds features, a workspace holds the checked-out code.

t2.text: Build: one run of a job

steps.say: Jenkins needs a compatible Java runtime, so check Java first.
Jenkins can also run in Docker: the web UI is mapped to port 8080 and its data is kept in a volume.
Open http://localhost:8080 and complete the setup wizard.
Once the wizard is finished, Jenkins is ready to create jobs.
A Jenkins job defines an automation task, for example a Freestyle Project.
Build triggers decide when a job runs. Manual: a developer starts it from Jenkins.
Poll SCM checks the repository periodically. A webhook is event-driven: GitHub tells Jenkins immediately.
A GitHub webhook is the usual choice: Jenkins starts as soon as someone pushes code or opens a pull request.
A pipeline defines a sequence of automated stages. Create a file named Jenkinsfile in the repository.
This pipeline has four stages: checkout, install dependencies, run tests and build the application.
Jenkins executes the stages in sequence.
If a stage fails, the later stages are normally skipped.
A Jenkinsfile stores the pipeline as code inside the application repository.
Declarative Pipeline gives a structured syntax. Each element has a clear job.
environment defines variables, and post runs success or failure actions after execution.
Keeping the Jenkinsfile in Git lets pipeline changes be reviewed and versioned together with the application code.
A team keeps a React frontend and a Node.js backend on GitHub and wants tests to run on every push.
GitHub Actions is an automation platform built into GitHub. Workflows run in response to repository events.
Unlike Jenkins, there is no separate server to install. It can test, build, scan, publish images and deploy.
A workflow is a YAML file stored in .github/workflows/.
An event decides when a workflow runs: push, pull_request, workflow_dispatch or schedule.
This workflow runs on pushes to main, on pull requests that target main, and on manual starts.
A workflow contains jobs, and a job contains steps that run commands or reusable actions.
A runner is the machine that executes a job. Here both jobs run on ubuntu-latest.
By default independent jobs run in parallel.
needs makes a job wait: with needs: test, build starts only after test succeeds.
A workflow is plain YAML: a name, the events, and jobs with steps.

l3.text: with → give inputs to an action

steps.say: uses executes a reusable GitHub Action: here checkout and setup-node.
run executes a shell command: install, test and build.
with supplies inputs to an action. Choose the Node.js version to match your application.
Workflows need configuration such as API endpoints. An env block avoids hardcoding values in every step.
Sensitive values belong in GitHub Actions Secrets, never written directly into workflow files.
Create the secret in repository or organization settings first, and never print it in workflow logs.
A workflow can produce files that must outlive the job, such as a React production build in dist/.
actions/upload-artifact stores the folder so another job, or you, can download it after the job ends.
To follow a run: open the Actions tab, select the workflow, open a run and inspect each step log.
Logs reveal dependency problems, test failures, configuration mistakes and build errors.

ok.text: Logs show why a step failed

steps.say: A developer changes the authentication endpoint of an application.
Login still works, but the change accidentally breaks registration.
If only login is tested by hand, the registration bug stays hidden until users hit it.
Automated tests run on every change, so the pipeline catches the problem before it is merged.
A unit test checks one function on its own. Here is a function that calculates an order total.
A Jest test calls the function and states the expected result.
The test passes. Unit tests should be small, focused and quick to run.
Integration tests check that several components work together: route, controller, hashing service and database.
End-to-end tests drive the app like a user, for example with Playwright or Cypress.

p.title: E2E test
lines: 5  log in with the new account

steps.say: Unit, integration and end-to-end tests serve different purposes. A reliable app usually uses all three.
Code coverage measures how much code your tests execute: 80 of 100 lines run means 80% line coverage.
High coverage does not prove the app is defect-free. Tests must also check meaningful behavior.
A quality gate lists conditions that must be met before code is accepted.
If the gate fails, the pipeline stops the change from reaching later stages.
SonarQube analyzes source code for code smells, potential bugs, vulnerabilities, duplication and maintainability problems.
A typical flow: push, CI builds and tests, SonarQube analyzes, a quality report is produced, the quality gate decides.
SonarQube integrates with Jenkins and GitHub Actions.
Modern apps depend on external packages such as Express and React, and those can contain known vulnerabilities.
npm audit reports the vulnerable packages.
npm audit fix can apply updates, but review them first because updates may cause compatibility problems.
Add scanning to CI, and use Dependabot alerts, so problems are found continuously instead of after an incident.

ok.text: Scan in CI, not after an incident

steps.say: On every pull request to main, one job validates the code before it can be merged.
The steps run in order: install, test, audit the dependencies, build.
If a required command fails, here the audit, the later stages do not run.
Once every check is green, the change can move on to the next stage.
Development is where developers implement and try new features.
Staging validates behavior under conditions similar to production.
Production is where real users use the application. A release goes there after approval.
Each environment has its own configuration, database, permissions and infrastructure, so unfinished work cannot reach real users.
An application runs as three instances, all on Version 1.
A rolling deployment replaces instances gradually. Instance A now runs Version 2.
Then B, then C, until every instance runs Version 2, without stopping the whole application.
In Kubernetes, kubectl set image starts a rolling update, and rollout status follows it.
Blue is the live production environment running Version 1. All users are on Blue.
Version 2 is deployed to Green and tested there, while users stay on Blue.
Once Green is validated, traffic is switched from Blue to Green.
If Green misbehaves, send users back to Blue. This works while Blue is still available and compatible.
A canary release sends a small share of traffic to the new version: 95% stays on Version 1, 5% goes to Version 2.
If the new version behaves well, its share grows: 25% to Version 2.
Then 50%, as long as the monitoring stays healthy.
Finally 100%. If problems had appeared, traffic would go back to the stable version.
A release can crash, slow responses down or break database compatibility.
A rollback restores the previous working version. In Kubernetes: rollout history, then rollout undo.
Reverting the app image does not undo an incompatible database migration, so plan for data too.
Release management adds versioning, notes, approvals, scheduling, monitoring and a rollback plan.
Rolling, blue-green and canary solve different operational problems.
The trade-offs differ: cost, speed of switching and how tightly the risk is limited.
The right choice depends on cost, traffic management, architecture and risk. Always keep a way to detect problems and respond.

ok.text: Always keep monitoring and a way back

steps.say: Two developers change a Kubernetes app by hand: one scales the replicas, the other changes the image.
The cluster drifts away from what Git says, and nobody can tell which is right.
GitOps makes Git the source of truth for the desired state. Changes go to Git, and automation syncs the cluster.
GitOps follows four principles. Declarative configuration describes the desired state of the system.
A typical workflow: a developer changes Git, a GitOps controller notices, and the cluster is updated.
Example: raising the replica count in a Deployment YAML and pushing it is enough. The change is traceable in Git.
Declarative configuration states what the system should look like, not every command needed to get there.
This declares three replicas. Kubernetes keeps three Pods running.
If a Pod fails, Kubernetes notices the difference from the desired state.
It creates a replacement to restore three replicas. GitOps keeps this YAML in Git and syncs it automatically.
Argo CD is a declarative GitOps continuous delivery tool for Kubernetes. Its UI and API server are how people use it.
The Repository Server fetches and renders configuration from Git.
The Application Controller compares desired and actual state and syncs the cluster.
Redis caches data for Argo CD operations. Sources can be plain manifests, Helm charts or Kustomize.
First create a namespace for Argo CD.
Applying the official install manifest creates the Argo CD components.
Check the Pods and wait until the components are running.
port-forward exposes the API server locally at https://localhost:8080. For production, configure authentication, TLS and network policies.

subtopics.title: Connect a Git Repository to Argo CD

steps.say: Argo CD needs an application definition: a name, plus where the configuration lives and where to deploy it.
--repo points to the Git repository that holds the Kubernetes manifests.
--dest-server and --dest-namespace say which cluster and namespace to deploy to.
--path selects the folder inside the repository. For private repositories, add credentials securely.
Argo CD compares the desired state in Git with the live state in Kubernetes. Here both say three replicas.
Someone scales the Deployment to five replicas by hand.
Argo CD reports OutOfSync. The difference is configuration drift.
Depending on the sync policy, Argo CD applies the desired state manually or automatically. Unknown means it cannot tell.
The image changed from Version 1 to Version 2, and the new version causes a problem.
A rollback is a Git operation: git revert creates a new commit that undoes the change.
Argo CD sees the new desired state in Git and syncs the cluster back to it.
History stays visible in Git. Change the desired state through Git, not with untracked manual edits to the cluster.
A developer pushes code to GitHub and GitHub Actions starts the pipeline.
It installs the dependencies and runs the automated tests. If a test fails, the pipeline stops before anything is published.
Then it builds the Docker images, pushes them to a registry and updates the Kubernetes manifests in Git.
Argo CD synchronizes the cluster, and the new version runs on Kubernetes.
A Dockerfile defines how the application image is built. Build and run it locally first.
A workflow in .github/workflows/docker-build.yml automates that build on every push to main.
Each push produces an image tagged with the commit SHA.

subtopics.title: Push Docker Images to a Container Registry

steps.say: A registry stores and distributes container images so deployment environments can pull them.
Tag the local image with the registry name first.
After logging in with credentials stored as secrets, push the image.
Tag images with unique identifiers such as the commit SHA, instead of relying only on latest.

ok.text: Tag with commit SHA, not only latest

steps.say: One workflow validates the code first: it runs on every push and every pull request to main.
Building the Docker image is the next step, but only after the tests passed.
An if condition limits the image build to pushes. A pull request only runs the tests.
A production workflow also needs registry login, publishing, security scanning and the right permissions.
Once the image is published, Kubernetes can run it. A Deployment declares two replicas of the backend.
kubectl apply creates the Deployment for an initial demonstration.
It starts the Pods. Check them and follow the rollout.
In a production GitOps workflow, update the manifest in Git and let Argo CD sync it instead.

n.text: In production: update Git, Argo CD syncs

steps.say: Instead of deploying straight from GitHub Actions, the pipeline builds and pushes the image, then updates a separate config repository.
Only the image reference changes in the manifest: from v1 to the new commit SHA.
Argo CD notices the repository change and synchronizes the Kubernetes cluster with the new desired state.
Responsibilities are separated: Actions builds, Git stores desired state, Argo CD syncs, Kubernetes runs.
A pipeline can fail at many points. Each stage has its typical problems.
For images and containers, list local images and all containers, including stopped ones.
For Kubernetes, check Pods, read the events with describe, and read container logs.
In Argo CD, inspect the sync status and events. A successful command is not the end: verify the app is healthy.

ok.text: Verify health, not just the command

steps.say: The final project connects everything: source, CI, tests, images, registry, manifests, Argo CD and health checks. First, the build half.
Then the delivery half: registry, manifests in Git, Argo CD sync and a health check.
A developer pushes a change. The pipeline validates and packages it, and the GitOps workflow delivers the new version to Kubernetes.
Version control, automation, containers, testing, Kubernetes and GitOps together deliver software reliably.
